s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A movie ticket booking system models cinemas with screens showing movies at scheduled shows, where users select seats and book them, with strict concurrency control so a seat is never sold twice. Core abstractions are Movie, Cinema, Screen, Seat, Show, Booking, and a seat-locking mechanism.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Booking a cinema seat is like reserving a specific numbered locker that thousands want at the same second. When Rajesh clicks seat A5 for the 9pm show, National Bank of India style systems place a short hold (lock) on A5 while he pays, so Priya cannot grab the same seat. If he does not pay in time, the hold expires and A5 is free again.

**One line to remember:** A movie booking system sells seats for shows with short-lived seat locks that prevent double-selling under heavy concurrency.

sections.s2_technical:
The central modelling challenge is concurrency. A `Show` is one screening of a `Movie` on a `Screen` at a time, and it holds the state of each `Seat`: AVAILABLE, LOCKED, or BOOKED. When a user selects seats, the system transitions them to LOCKED with a short expiry, typically a few minutes, during which only that user can confirm.

If payment succeeds within the window, the seats become BOOKED and a `Booking` is created; if the window expires, a background sweeper returns them to AVAILABLE. This two-phase approach — lock then confirm — is what every real platform uses.

```java
boolean locked = show.lockSeats(List.of("A5", "A6"), userId);
```

The lock must be atomic: checking and setting the seat state has to happen under a lock or an atomic compare-and-set, otherwise two users both see AVAILABLE and both lock. In distributed deployments I use a Redis lock keyed by show and seat with a TTL. The senior nuance is that the expiry TTL is essential; without it, abandoned carts would freeze inventory forever.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A blockbuster goes on sale and Rajesh and Priya both click seat A5 for the same 9pm show within the same second. Exactly one must win the seat; the other must be told it is gone. This is exactly the atomic seat-locking logic.

Problem 2 — Rajesh locks A5 but abandons payment. The seat must not be frozen forever. This is exactly why locks carry a short expiry.

The code defines `SeatStatus`, a `Show` with atomic seat locking and booking, and a `BookingService`, with a demo where Rajesh locks and books a seat while a second attempt on the same seat fails.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: show SHOW-9PM with seats A5, A6, A7 all available; Rajesh and Priya both want A5.

Step 1: Rajesh calls `lockSeats([A5])`; under the lock A5 is AVAILABLE, so it becomes LOCKED and recorded as his. Step 2: Priya calls `lockSeats([A5])`; under the same lock A5 is now LOCKED, so the method returns false immediately. Step 3: the demo logs that Rajesh won and Priya lost. Step 4: Rajesh calls `confirm([A5])`, which checks he holds the lock and flips A5 to BOOKED. The seat is now permanently his.

```
Oct 31 22:14 INFO MOVIE: Rajesh locked [A5]
Oct 31 22:14 INFO MOVIE: Rajesh locked=true Priya locked=false
Oct 31 22:14 INFO MOVIE: Rajesh booked [A5]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I design a movie ticket booking system, I treat concurrency as the first-class problem, because the entire difficulty is making sure a single seat is never sold to two people during a blockbuster rush. A Show is one screening of a Movie on a Screen at a time, and it tracks each seat as available, locked, or booked.

I use a two-phase approach that every real platform relies on: lock then confirm. When a user selects seats, I atomically move them from available to locked with a short expiry of a few minutes, during which only that user can confirm. If the payment succeeds within that window the seats become booked and I create the booking; if the window expires, a background sweeper returns the seats to available so an abandoned cart never freezes inventory.

The atomicity of the lock is everything. Checking that a seat is available and setting it to locked must happen as one indivisible step, otherwise two users both see available and both lock the same seat. In a single node I use a lock; in a distributed deployment I use a Redis lock keyed by show and seat with a time-to-live, which gives me both atomicity and automatic expiry.

The remaining pieces are straightforward: payment through a payment strategy, cancellation that releases seats back to available, and ratings after the show. The senior insight I bring is that the time-to-live on the lock is not optional detail but core correctness, because without it abandoned selections would permanently starve inventory. In my banking work at National Bank of India, this is the same discipline I use when many clients contend for a single limited resource, where I lock with a timeout, confirm on payment, and release automatically on abandonment.
